mcqs.question: A multi-tenant application has a bug where one query path forgets its `WHERE tenant_id = ?` filter. With Postgres row-level security policies configured on the table, what happens?
options: The query fails with a syntax error since RLS requires every query to include a tenant_id filter explicitly
RLS only applies to INSERT and UPDATE statements, so the missing filter still leaks rows on this SELECT
The application must catch this itself in a try/except block; RLS provides no protection here
The database itself enforces the row filter regardless of the application query, so the buggy query still can't see another tenant's rows
mcqs.explanation: Row-level security attaches the filtering policy at the database level, so it's enforced even when the application query itself forgot the equivalent WHERE clause — that's the entire point of RLS as defense-in-depth. It doesn't require the application to write the filter, doesn't only apply to writes, and doesn't rely on application-level error handling.

mcqs.question: A developer fixes a SQL injection vulnerability by adding code that escapes single quotes in user input before concatenating it into the query string. Is this a sufficient fix?
options: Yes, escaping quotes eliminates SQL injection entirely and permanently
No, it also requires disabling autocommit for the affected queries
Only if the database is MySQL; Postgres requires a different escaping approach
No — manual escaping is easy to get subtly wrong or miss in another code path; parameterized queries remove the risk structurally instead of relying on correct escaping everywhere
mcqs.explanation: Escaping can reduce risk but is fragile — it's easy to miss an edge case, an encoding issue, or a different code path that skips it; parameterized queries avoid the entire class of bug by never interpreting user input as SQL syntax in the first place. This isn't related to autocommit, and it's not a database-specific limitation of one engine over another.

mcqs.question: An application opens a brand-new database connection for every incoming HTTP request and closes it when the request finishes. Under moderate concurrent load, what problem is this most likely to cause?
options: The per-request connection setup overhead and per-connection memory cost can exhaust the database's max connection limit and add latency to every request
SQL injection vulnerabilities, since each connection has different escaping rules
Data corruption, since concurrent connections cannot safely coexist
Slower query planning, since the query planner caches plans per connection
mcqs.explanation: Opening and closing a connection per request pays real setup cost (handshake, auth, and on Postgres a new backend process) on every request and can exhaust the connection limit under load — exactly what pooling exists to prevent. This has nothing to do with SQL injection or data corruption, and while plan caching is a real Postgres nuance, it isn't the primary problem this pattern causes.

mcqs.question: A page renders 50 blog posts and, for each post, runs a separate query to fetch that post's author. What is the most direct fix for this N+1 pattern?
options: Cache the entire page indefinitely to avoid re-running any queries
Replace the 50 per-post author queries with a single query using a JOIN or a WHERE author_id IN (...) covering all 50 posts at once
Increase the connection pool size so the 50 queries run faster in parallel
Switch the 50 queries to run asynchronously so they don't block each other
mcqs.explanation: The fix for N+1 is reducing query count, not making the same number of queries faster or more parallel — a single JOIN or batched IN query replaces 50 round trips with one. A bigger pool or async execution both still issue 50 separate queries and don't address the underlying inefficiency, and indefinite caching sidesteps the problem rather than fixing the query pattern.

mcqs.question: A company's application database account has full admin privileges 'to keep things simple.' A SQL injection bug is later found and exploited. What does the attacker gain as a direct result of that privilege choice?
options: Nothing beyond what a properly scoped account would have allowed, since injection severity doesn't depend on account privileges
Access limited to just the tables the injected query directly referenced
Only read access, since admin privileges don't include the ability to modify data through injection
The full scope of the admin account — dropping tables, reading every tenant's data, altering permissions — because the compromised query runs with whatever privileges the account holds
mcqs.explanation: An attacker exploiting injection inherits exactly the privileges of the database account the vulnerable code uses — an admin account turns an application bug into a total database compromise. Injection severity absolutely depends on account privileges, and admin access includes both read and write capability well beyond the tables a specific query references.

mcqs.question: An application's requests are timing out waiting on the database, but the database server's own CPU and query latency metrics look completely normal. What should you check next?
options: The database's disk I/O metrics, since CPU alone can't reveal disk contention
Whether the query planner is choosing bad execution plans
The connection pool's own metrics — checked-out connections, wait queue depth, and wait time — since pool exhaustion produces this exact symptom independent of database health
Whether the database needs a larger instance size
mcqs.explanation: Pool exhaustion — every connection checked out, none returned quickly enough — makes requests hang waiting for a connection even when the database itself is healthy and lightly loaded, which matches the symptom exactly. Disk I/O, query plans, and instance sizing are all database-side concerns that wouldn't explain healthy database metrics alongside application-side timeouts.
